task_3.title: Add adjacent-item access in loop contexts
task_3.description: The 2.10 update adds loop-context support for accessing the previous and next item during iteration. Templates can now inspect neighboring values directly from the loop object, with missing neighbors represented as undefined values, and the same behavior applies in regular, recursive, and asynchronous loops.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that loop contexts expose adjacent items during iteration so templates can read the previous and next element from the current loop. Ensure that boundary cases behave safely by returning an undefined value when no previous or next element exists. Ensure that this behavior is consistent for standard loops, recursive loops, and asynchronous loops.

expectation.grounded: A `{% for %}` loop context in 2.10 must provide `loop.previtem` and `loop.nextitem`. For any iteration after the first, `loop.previtem` must resolve to the immediately preceding item from the same loop context; on the first iteration it must resolve to an undefined value. For any iteration before the last, `loop.nextitem` must resolve to the immediately following item from the same loop context; on the last iteration it must resolve to an undefined value. The same observable behavior must be available when using recursive loop rendering and async iteration.
expectation.conceptual: Templates should be able to look one item backward or forward within a loop by reading `loop.previtem` and `loop.nextitem`. These properties should behave predictably at the start and end of the loop by appearing undefined instead of failing, and they should work the same way regardless of whether the loop is normal, recursive, or async.

constraints.grounded: The added loop-context properties must not change the item yielded for the current iteration, the loop index/depth semantics, or loop termination behavior. `previtem` and `nextitem` must describe neighbors within the current loop scope only, including within each recursive level, and absent neighbors must remain observable as undefined values rather than concrete sentinel data.
constraints.conceptual: Adding adjacent-item access must not alter how loops iterate today. Existing loop ordering and nesting behavior should stay intact, and neighbor lookups should stay local to the current loop level while treating missing neighbors as ordinary undefined values.

behavior: Loop contexts expose a `previtem` property representing the immediately previous item in the current iteration sequence.
Loop contexts expose a `nextitem` property representing the immediately next item in the current iteration sequence.
On the first iteration, `loop.previtem` evaluates as undefined instead of a real item.
On the last iteration, `loop.nextitem` evaluates as undefined instead of a real item.
Recursive loops maintain `previtem` and `nextitem` relative to the current recursive loop level rather than another level's sequence.
Asynchronous loop contexts provide the same `previtem` and `nextitem` semantics as synchronous loop contexts.
acceptance_criteria: When iterating over a sequence with at least two items, each iteration after the first should expose the immediately preceding item through `loop.previtem`.
When iterating over a sequence with at least two items, each iteration before the last should expose the immediately following item through `loop.nextitem`.
When rendering the first iteration of a loop, `loop.previtem` should be treated as undefined.
When rendering the last iteration of a loop, `loop.nextitem` should be treated as undefined.
When a loop is recursive, adjacent-item access should reflect neighbors from the current recursive level only.
When a loop runs in async mode, `loop.previtem` and `loop.nextitem` should behave the same as in non-async loops.

task_2.title: Add builtin membership and comparison template tests
task_2.description: The 2.10 upgrade adds a builtin `in` template test for membership checks, especially for use with `select` and `reject`, and broadens builtin test support so common comparison operators and aliases are available as named tests with consistent evaluation behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can perform membership checks through a builtin `in` test and can rely on builtin comparison tests being available through standard operator-style aliases when upgrading to 2.10.

expectation.grounded: Jinja2 2.10 should expose an `in` test in the builtin test registry so expressions such as `value is in sequence` work the same way as Python membership checks and can be used with features like `select` and `reject`. Builtin comparison tests should also be available through symbolic and named aliases for equality and ordering, including `==`/`eq`/`equalto`, `!=`/`ne`, `>`/`gt`/`greaterthan`, `>=`/`ge`, `<`/`lt`/`lessthan`, and `<=`/`le`. Builtin tests should evaluate correctly when invoked with constant operands and constant keyword or variadic arguments, and unavailable tests or non-constant inputs in constant-only evaluation contexts should remain non-constant rather than producing a successful constant result.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, template authors should be able to express membership checks directly with a builtin `in` test and use standard equality and ordering test names interchangeably. These tests should behave predictably for normal rendering and for expressions composed entirely of constant values.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must preserve Python-style membership semantics across supported container types and preserve the existing behavior that unknown tests do not become valid implicitly. Comparison aliases must remain behaviorally equivalent within each alias group, and test evaluation must not report a constant result when argument expansion or evaluation cannot be resolved safely.
constraints.conceptual: Do not change the meaning of membership or comparison checks beyond aligning them with normal template and Python expectations. Equivalent test names should stay interchangeable, and unsupported or non-resolvable cases should fail in the existing safe way rather than silently changing meaning.

behavior: A new builtin `in` test returns whether the left-hand value is contained in the right-hand operand.
The `in` test is intended to be usable anywhere builtin tests are accepted, including filtering workflows such as `select` and `reject`.
Builtin comparison tests are available through symbolic and word-based aliases for equality, inequality, greater-than, greater-than-or-equal, less-than, and less-than-or-equal checks.
Aliases within the same comparison family produce the same observable boolean result for the same operands.
Builtin tests can be resolved for constant expressions when their target value and supplied arguments are constant and evaluable.
acceptance_criteria: When a template evaluates `value is in collection`, it should return `True` if `value` is a member of `collection` and `False` otherwise.
When `select` or `reject` is used with the builtin `in` test, membership filtering should follow the same truth value as direct `is in` evaluation.
When a template uses any alias in the equality family (`==`, `eq`, `equalto`) with the same operands, each alias should produce the same result.

When a template uses any alias in the inequality or ordering families (`!=`/`ne`, `>`/`gt`/`greaterthan`, `>=`/`ge`, `<`/`lt`/`lessthan`, `<=`/`le`), each alias group should produce the same result as its corresponding comparison.
When a builtin test is applied to expressions made entirely of constant values, it should behave the same as normal runtime evaluation instead of diverging because of constant-expression handling.

task_1.title: Add OverlayScope support for extension-defined overlay contexts
task_1.description: Version 2.10 adds a new extension node, OverlayScope, so extensions can render a body against a dynamically supplied mapping while still falling back to the surrounding derived context for other variable lookups. The compiler and symbol tracking now treat this as an isolated, intentionally unoptimized scope and preserve that derived-context behavior inside nested scoped rendering.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that extensions can create an overlay scope that injects arbitrary variables for a section of template output while preserving lookup of variables from the surrounding derived context.

expectation.grounded: Jinja2 2.10 should expose `jinja2.nodes.OverlayScope` as an extension statement node with `context` and `body` fields. When an extension returns this node, the `context` expression must be evaluated as a dictionary or dictionary-like object whose entries become the active variables for the overlay body, and unresolved names inside that body must continue resolving through the derived parent context. Nested scoped rendering created from within the overlay must derive from the active overlay context rather than reverting to the original root context.
expectation.conceptual: Extension authors should be able to wrap part of a template in a special scope backed by a dynamic mapping. Inside that scope, template code should see the injected variables first, while still being able to access other variables that were already available outside the scope, including inside nested scoped constructs.

constraints.grounded: The `OverlayScope.context` value must be a dictionary or dictionary-like object. The overlay body must be treated as an isolated, unoptimized scope so compile-time symbol assumptions do not prevent access to dynamically supplied names. Outside an `OverlayScope`, existing context resolution behavior should remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: The new scope must accept mapping-like overlay data, allow dynamic names without relying on compile-time declarations, and avoid changing normal rendering behavior for templates that do not use the feature.

behavior: A new statement node named `OverlayScope` is available for extensions in version 2.10.
Rendering an `OverlayScope` body creates a derived context and replaces that scope's active variable mapping with the evaluated overlay mapping.
Variable lookups inside the overlay body resolve through the overlay context object, so names missing from the overlay mapping can still be resolved from the surrounding derived context.
The overlay body is compiled as an isolated scope, reflecting that injected variable names may only be known at render time.
Scoped rendering entered from within an overlay uses the current overlay-derived context as its parent context, preserving overlay lookup behavior in nested scoped regions.
acceptance_criteria: When an extension returns an `OverlayScope` whose overlay mapping defines a variable used in the body, rendering should use the overlay-provided value within that body.
When the overlay body references a variable that is not present in the overlay mapping but is available from the surrounding render context, rendering should still resolve that variable successfully.

When the overlay body contains nested scoped rendering, that nested rendering should continue to resolve names through the same overlay-derived context instead of losing access to the overlay behavior.
When templates do not use `OverlayScope`, their existing variable resolution behavior should remain unchanged.

task_4.title: Add loop.changed value-change detection
task_4.description: The update adds a new loop-context helper, `loop.changed(*values)`, so templates can detect when a value or value group differs from the previous check inside the same loop without maintaining manual state.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that template loop contexts provide a built-in way to detect whether one or more observed values have changed since the previous `loop.changed(...)` check, so templates can react to group boundaries or repeated values without manual bookkeeping.

expectation.grounded: Expose `changed(*values)` on loop context objects as `loop.changed(...)`. It should return a boolean indicating whether the current positional argument tuple differs from the tuple passed to the immediately preceding `loop.changed(...)` call in the same loop context. The first call in a loop context should report a change, and repeated calls with the same tuple should report no change until a different tuple is supplied.
expectation.conceptual: Templates should be able to ask the loop whether the currently observed value set is different from the last observed value set, and receive a simple true/false answer that can drive rendering decisions.

constraints.grounded: The feature must be additive to existing loop-context behavior, keep change-tracking state scoped to an individual loop context, and support zero or more positional values as the observed input. Comparison must reflect the full supplied value set for the most recent `loop.changed(...)` call rather than relying on external template state.
constraints.conceptual: This should work as a self-contained loop helper that does not alter normal loop semantics or require users to manually store previous values.

behavior: `loop.changed(*values)` is available during loop iteration as part of the loop context.
The first `loop.changed(...)` call in a loop context returns `True`.
A later `loop.changed(...)` call returns `False` when its supplied values match those from the most recent prior `loop.changed(...)` call in the same loop context.
A later `loop.changed(...)` call returns `True` when its supplied values differ from those from the most recent prior `loop.changed(...)` call in the same loop context.
Change detection is stateful within a loop context and resets when a new loop context starts.
acceptance_criteria: When a template calls `loop.changed(item)` on each pass through a loop, it should return `True` for the first item and again whenever `item` differs from the value passed on the previous `loop.changed(item)` call.
When consecutive `loop.changed(...)` calls in the same loop context receive identical values, the later call should return `False`.

When `loop.changed(...)` is called multiple times before the next iteration, each call should compare against the immediately preceding `loop.changed(...)` call rather than an earlier iteration boundary.
When `loop.changed(a, b, ...)` is called with multiple values, the method should evaluate change based on the combined argument set.
When a new loop context begins, its first `loop.changed(...)` call should return `True` regardless of what was observed in a previous loop.

task_5.title: Support namespace state and filtered block set assignments
task_5.description: The upgrade adds a built-in `namespace` helper for storing mutable template state across scopes through dotted `set` assignments, and extends block-style `set` so captured content can be filtered before assignment.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can create mutable namespace state, assign to namespace attributes with the `set` tag so values can survive inner scopes such as loops and macros, and apply filters to block-captured `set` content before the result is stored.

expectation.grounded: Expose a default `namespace` global that creates a `Namespace` object, optionally initialized from mapping data and keyword arguments. Within the `set` tag, accept dotted assignment targets such as `ns.value` for both inline and block assignments, writing into the referenced `Namespace`. If the dotted assignment target does not resolve to a `Namespace`, rendering should raise `TemplateRuntimeError`. Allow block-form `set` assignments to include filters so the captured content is transformed before storage.
expectation.conceptual: Template authors should be able to keep mutable state in a dedicated namespace object, update it from nested scopes, and read the final attributes later in the template. Block `set` assignments should support filter pipelines on captured content, and invalid dotted assignment on ordinary values should fail clearly at runtime.

constraints.grounded: Limit dotted assignment targets to `set` usage and do not change ordinary dotted expressions into general-purpose write operations. Reject attribute writes when the base value is not a `Namespace`. Preserve existing `set` capture behavior except for the added ability to filter block-assigned content before it is stored.
constraints.conceptual: The feature should add safe mutable cross-scope state without changing normal attribute lookup semantics, and existing templates should behave the same unless they opt into namespace assignment or filtered block capture.

behavior: The default template global namespace includes a `namespace` callable that creates a mutable object whose members are read through attribute access.
`namespace()` accepts initial values from mapping input and keyword arguments, and later assignments can add or replace attributes on that object.
The `set` tag accepts dotted targets in the form `name.attribute`, and assigning to such a target updates the referenced namespace object instead of rebinding a local variable.
Mutations made through a namespace object remain visible after inner scopes complete because the same namespace instance is updated rather than shadowed.
If a dotted `set` target resolves to a non-namespace value, rendering raises `TemplateRuntimeError` instead of silently accepting the assignment.
Block-form `set` assignments may include filters, and the stored value reflects the captured block output after the declared filters are applied.
acceptance_criteria: When a template creates `ns = namespace()` and later assigns `ns.value` with the `set` tag, reading `ns.value` afterward should return the assigned value.
When a namespace attribute is modified inside a loop or macro and read after that scope ends, the rendered output should reflect the modified value.
When `namespace()` is called with initial mapping data and keyword values, those attributes should be readable and remain available alongside later namespace assignments.
When block-form `set` syntax is used with one or more filters, the assigned variable should contain the filtered captured content.
When a dotted `set` assignment targets an object that is not a namespace instance, rendering should fail with `TemplateRuntimeError`.

task_6.title: Add whitespace trimming controls for trans blocks
task_6.description: The 2.10 upgrade adds translation-block whitespace normalization so multi-line `{% trans %}` content can produce cleaner message strings. Trimming can be enabled per block or made the default through the i18n policy, while still allowing blocks to preserve original whitespace when needed.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `{% trans %}` blocks support an opt-in whitespace-trimming mode, and that applications can enable that behavior by default across translation blocks while preserving a way to keep original whitespace for specific blocks.

expectation.grounded: The internationalization extension should accept `trimmed` on a `{% trans %}` block to normalize the singular and plural message text by stripping leading and trailing whitespace and collapsing whitespace surrounding line breaks into single spaces. If no per-block modifier is provided, the extension should consult the `ext.i18n.trimmed` environment policy, which defaults to `False`. When the policy enables trimming globally, `{% trans notrimmed %}` should keep the original block whitespace. Extraction through `babel_extract` should honor the trimming policy when the extractor option `trimmed` is enabled.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to write multi-line translation blocks without leaking template indentation and line breaks into translated message strings. They should be able to turn this on for one block or configure it as the default for all translation blocks, while retaining an explicit opt-out for blocks that need exact whitespace.

constraints.grounded: Whitespace normalization should affect only the message text assembled from `{% trans %}` and pluralized `trans` blocks; it must not change variable references, pluralization requirements, or the default behavior when no trimming option or policy is set. Explicit per-block trimming directives should take precedence over the environment default.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must improve whitespace handling for translation content without changing unrelated translation semantics. Existing templates should continue to behave the same unless trimming is explicitly requested or globally enabled, and explicit block-level intent should override the default.

behavior: A `{% trans trimmed %}` block normalizes surrounding whitespace in its generated translation string by removing outer whitespace and replacing whitespace around embedded line breaks with single spaces.
The same whitespace normalization applies to both the singular and plural message text produced from a pluralized translation block.
If a `{% trans %}` block does not specify `trimmed` or `notrimmed`, whitespace handling falls back to the `ext.i18n.trimmed` environment policy.
The default value of `ext.i18n.trimmed` is disabled, so unmodified translation blocks preserve prior whitespace behavior.
When the environment policy enables trimming globally, `{% trans notrimmed %}` preserves the original block whitespace instead of applying normalization.
When extraction is configured with the `trimmed` option, extracted translation messages use the same trimming policy as runtime parsing.
acceptance_criteria: When a multi-line `{% trans trimmed %}` block is parsed, the resulting translation message should not include leading or trailing whitespace from the block and should collapse indentation-separated line breaks to single spaces.
When a pluralized translation block uses `trimmed`, both the singular and plural messages should be normalized consistently.
When `ext.i18n.trimmed` is `False` and no block modifier is given, `{% trans %}` blocks should preserve their previous whitespace behavior.
When `ext.i18n.trimmed` is `True` and no block modifier is given, `{% trans %}` blocks should be trimmed by default.
When `ext.i18n.trimmed` is `True` but a block uses `{% trans notrimmed %}`, that block should preserve original whitespace instead of using the global trimmed behavior.
When Babel extraction runs with the `trimmed` option enabled, the extracted translation strings should reflect the same whitespace normalization behavior expected from trimmed translation blocks.

task_7.title: Preserve runtime randomness for the Jinja random filter
task_7.description: Jinja 2.10 fixes the `random` template filter so it is evaluated during each render instead of being folded into a constant when a template is compiled. This restores expected dynamic behavior for repeated renders while preserving the existing undefined result for empty sequences.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates using the `random` filter produce a fresh random selection each time they are rendered, rather than reusing a value that was fixed when the template was compiled.

expectation.grounded: The `random` filter must remain a public template filter and be evaluated at render time for every render invocation, including when it is applied to compile-time constant values inside the template. Applying `random` to a non-empty sequence should select one item from that sequence at runtime. Applying `random` to an empty sequence should continue to return the active environment's undefined result for that condition.
expectation.conceptual: Templates that use `|random` should behave as dynamic content. Re-rendering the same compiled template should be able to return different items from the same input, while empty inputs should still behave like an undefined value instead of causing a crash.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the public `random` filter contract apart from preventing compile-time constant folding or inlining of its result. Preserve the existing empty-sequence behavior of producing an undefined value through the current environment.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should be narrowly scoped to restoring true runtime randomness and keeping existing error semantics for empty inputs. Users should not need to rewrite templates that already use `|random`.

behavior: A compiled template that contains `|random` must perform a new random selection each time it is rendered.
Using `|random` on a literal or otherwise constant expression in a template must no longer freeze one chosen value at compile time.
Using `|random` on an empty sequence must continue to produce the environment-defined undefined result for that case.
acceptance_criteria: When the same compiled template containing `|random` is rendered multiple times with a non-empty sequence, it should evaluate the filter at render time rather than replaying a compile-time-fixed result.
When `|random` is applied to a constant value inside a template, repeated renders should still reflect runtime randomness.
When `|random` receives an empty sequence, rendering should return an undefined value consistent with the active environment.
When `|random` receives a non-empty sequence, rendering should return one member of the provided sequence.

task_8.title: Add a unique filter and align sequence comparison behavior
task_8.description: Version 2.10 adds a new `unique` template filter for removing duplicates while preserving first-seen order, and it aligns sequence-oriented filters so `sort`, `min`, and `max` consistently support attribute-based lookup and default case-insensitive handling for string values.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can remove duplicate items with a `unique` filter while preserving the first occurrence of each item, and ensure that sequence comparison filters apply consistent attribute-aware and case-handling semantics across `unique`, `sort`, `min`, and `max`.

expectation.grounded: Expose a `unique` filter in the public Jinja filter set. `unique` must accept `case_sensitive` and `attribute` arguments, preserve input order, and suppress later items whose comparison key matches an earlier item. By default, string comparisons for `unique` and `sort` must be case-insensitive, and `sort` must apply that normalization after resolving an optional `attribute`. `min` and `max` must also accept `case_sensitive` and `attribute`, compare using the same attribute/key semantics, and return Jinja undefined for empty iterables rather than raising.
expectation.conceptual: Template authors should be able to deduplicate lists directly in templates, including lists of objects, without losing the original order of the first matching entries. Sequence filters that compare values should behave consistently: they should optionally compare object attributes, treat string case insensitively by default unless requested otherwise, and handle empty input without crashing.

constraints.grounded: Do not reorder deduplicated output beyond keeping the first encountered item for each distinct comparison key. Only string values should be normalized for case-insensitive comparison; other value types should retain their normal comparison behavior. Attribute-based comparison must remain optional and must not break direct value comparison when no attribute is provided. Empty-input handling for `min` and `max` must remain undefined-producing behavior rather than an exception.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should add deduplication and comparison flexibility without changing the basic shape of existing template pipelines. It must preserve stable ordering, avoid surprising case transformations on non-string data, and degrade safely on empty sequences.

behavior: `unique` becomes available as a built-in template filter.
`unique` emits only the first occurrence of each item according to its comparison key and preserves original iteration order.
When `case_sensitive` is omitted or false, `unique` and `sort` compare string values without distinguishing case.
When `case_sensitive` is true, case-distinct string values remain distinct for `unique` and are ordered using case-sensitive comparison for `sort`, `min`, and `max`.
`unique(attribute=...)` deduplicates objects or mappings by the resolved attribute value instead of the full item.
`sort(attribute=...)` derives its sort key from the resolved attribute value and then applies case normalization only when case-insensitive string comparison is in effect.
`min(attribute=...)` and `max(attribute=...)` select the item whose resolved attribute value is respectively smallest or largest.
`min` and `max` return Jinja undefined on empty iterables.
acceptance_criteria: When a template applies `unique` to a sequence containing repeated values, it should output each distinct value only once and keep the first-seen ordering.
When a template applies `unique` to strings that differ only by letter case, it should collapse them by default and keep them separate only when case-sensitive mode is enabled.
When a template applies `unique(attribute=...)` to a sequence of objects or mappings, it should preserve only the first item for each distinct attribute value.
When a template applies `sort` with `attribute=...`, it should sort by that attribute and treat string case insensitively unless case-sensitive mode is requested.
When a template applies `min` or `max` to a sequence of strings, the selected item should reflect case-insensitive comparison by default and case-sensitive comparison when explicitly requested.
When a template applies `min(attribute=...)` or `max(attribute=...)` to a sequence of objects or mappings, it should return the original item with the lowest or highest attribute value.
When a template applies `min` or `max` to an empty iterable, it should produce undefined behavior rather than raising a runtime failure.

task_9.title: Add built-in min and max template filters
task_9.description: Jinja 2.10 adds built-in `min` and `max` filters so templates can compute aggregate values without custom filters, while matching existing built-in comparison semantics for case handling and attribute-based lookup.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Jinja 2.10 exposes built-in `min` and `max` template filters for sequences, and that these filters behave consistently for strings and object collections without requiring application-defined replacements.

expectation.grounded: Register `min` and `max` as built-in Jinja filters. Each filter must accept an iterable plus optional `case_sensitive` and `attribute` arguments. By default, string comparisons are case-insensitive; when `case_sensitive` is true, original string casing must affect ordering. When `attribute` is provided, the selected result must be the original item whose resolved attribute is minimal or maximal. If the iterable is empty, the filter must return an undefined value rather than raising from the aggregation step.
expectation.conceptual: Templates should be able to ask for the smallest or largest item directly with `min` and `max`. These filters should work predictably for plain values and collections of objects, compare strings case-insensitively unless explicitly told otherwise, and fail gracefully on empty input.

constraints.grounded: The filters must preserve the original selected item instead of returning only the compared key. Attribute-based lookup must follow the same public semantics used by other built-in filters that support `attribute`. The default comparison mode must not treat uppercase and lowercase strings as distinct ordering keys unless `case_sensitive` is enabled.
constraints.conceptual: The new filters should fit the library's existing template behavior: they should select from the input data itself, honor the same attribute-selection rules users already expect, and avoid introducing surprising case-ordering changes unless requested.

behavior: A template can call `min` on a sequence to obtain the smallest item and `max` to obtain the largest item.
For string inputs, comparisons are case-insensitive by default, so ordering is based on normalized casing rather than raw character case.
When `case_sensitive=true` is supplied, string comparisons use original casing and may produce a different minimum or maximum than the default mode.
When `attribute` is supplied, comparison is performed on the resolved attribute value, but the filter returns the original object or item from the sequence.
When the input sequence is empty, the filter produces an undefined result instead of throwing a direct aggregation error during template evaluation.
acceptance_criteria: When a template renders `min` over a non-empty numeric sequence, it should produce the smallest numeric item from that sequence.
When a template renders `max` over a non-empty numeric sequence, it should produce the largest numeric item from that sequence.
When `min` or `max` is used on strings without `case_sensitive=true`, it should compare values without distinguishing letter case.
When `case_sensitive=true` is provided, `min` and `max` should reflect case-sensitive string ordering.
When `attribute` is provided for a sequence of objects or mappings, `min` and `max` should choose the item with the smallest or largest resolved attribute value and return that original item.
When `min` or `max` is applied to an empty sequence, template rendering should receive an undefined result rather than an unhandled aggregation exception.

task_10.title: Support comparison operator tests by alias and symbol
task_10.description: Jinja 2.10 expands template test syntax so comparison checks can be referenced by short names and operator symbols in direct `is` expressions and test-driven filters, while preserving existing long-form names and adding membership-test support.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can use comparison operator tests through both symbolic and short-name forms, and that these test names behave consistently anywhere Jinja resolves tests, without breaking existing long-form aliases.

expectation.grounded: Jinja test lookup should expose comparison tests under `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and the short aliases `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, in addition to preserving the existing long names `equalto`, `greaterthan`, and `lessthan`. These names must be accepted in direct `is` test expressions and in APIs that resolve tests by name, such as selector-style filters. The built-in test registry should also include an `in` test for membership checks. Test expressions with constant operands should preserve the same boolean result when treated as constant expressions.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.10 should be able to write Jinja tests with familiar comparison operator names or symbols, and those forms should work the same way in normal template conditions and in filter-based selection. Existing comparison test names must keep working, and membership checks through a test-style `in` form should be available.

constraints.grounded: Existing supported comparison test names must remain valid and continue to produce the same outcomes. Adding symbolic and short-name aliases must not change the meaning of equivalent comparisons, and unresolved or invalid test calls should continue to fail through normal test-resolution behavior rather than silently succeeding.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must be additive: new comparison spellings should expand what template authors can write, not alter how previous templates behave. Equivalent comparison forms should stay semantically aligned, and invalid test usage should still surface as an error instead of producing misleading results.

behavior: Template tests now recognize symbolic comparison names `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=`.
Template tests now recognize short comparison aliases `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, and `ge`.
Existing long-form comparison test names such as `equalto`, `greaterthan`, and `lessthan` remain available.
Comparison test names can be resolved in direct `is` expressions as well as in filters that accept a test name argument, such as selection filters.
A built-in `in` test is available for membership checks against a sequence or container.
When a test expression and its arguments are constant, Jinja can treat the test result as a constant without changing the rendered boolean outcome.
acceptance_criteria: When a template uses `is eq`, `is ne`, `is lt`, `is le`, `is gt`, or `is ge`, it should evaluate the same way as the corresponding comparison.
When a template uses symbolic test names such as `is <=` or `is ==`, it should parse successfully and return the same boolean result as the equivalent named comparison test.
When a selector-style filter receives a comparison test name by symbol or short alias, it should apply that comparison to filter items correctly.
When a template continues to use `equalto`, `greaterthan`, or `lessthan`, it should keep producing the same results as before the upgrade.
When a template uses the built-in `in` test, it should return `True` only when the left-hand value is contained in the right-hand sequence or container.
When a test expression is composed entirely of constant values, it should render the same boolean result as the equivalent non-constant form.

task_11.title: Reject malformed from-import template syntax
task_11.description: Jinja 2.10 tightens validation for `{% from ... import ... %}` statements so invalid import lists are no longer silently accepted. Templates that previously compiled despite missing imported names or trailing and repeated commas must now fail with a syntax error, including cases that previously behaved differently depending on whether `with context` was present.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that malformed `{% from ... import ... %}` statements are rejected consistently. Ensure that the import list always contains valid imported names, and that empty imports, trailing commas, repeated commas, or comma-separated gaps no longer compile silently.

expectation.grounded: When Jinja parses a `{% from template import ... %}` statement, the import section must consist of one or more `name` tokens separated by single commas. The parser should reject missing names at the start of the import list, after any comma, and at the end of the list. This stricter validation must apply whether or not the statement uses `with context`, and malformed statements should surface as template syntax failures rather than being accepted.
expectation.conceptual: Users should only be able to import explicitly named symbols in `{% from ... import ... %}` statements. If the import clause is incomplete or contains stray commas, template compilation should fail consistently instead of accepting invalid syntax in some forms.

constraints.grounded: Valid `{% from ... import name %}` and `{% from ... import name1, name2 %}` statements must continue to compile. The optional `with context` form must remain supported for valid imports, but it must not permit malformed import lists that would otherwise be invalid. The change is limited to syntax validation of `from ... import ...` parsing behavior.
constraints.conceptual: Correct import statements must keep working as before, including the context-carrying form. The upgrade should only remove accidental acceptance of invalid template syntax and should not change the meaning of valid imports.

behavior: A `{% from ... import ... %}` statement now requires at least one imported name.
After each comma in the import list, another imported name must appear immediately; repeated commas or comma-created gaps are invalid.
A trailing comma at the end of the import list is invalid, even when the statement does not use `with context`.
The validation rules for malformed import lists are now consistent between plain `from ... import ...` statements and the `with context` variant.
Malformed `from ... import ...` statements should fail during template parsing or compilation with a template syntax error instead of compiling successfully.
acceptance_criteria: When a template contains `{% from ... import name %}` or `{% from ... import name1, name2 %}`, it should compile successfully.
When a template contains `{% from ... import %}`, it should fail with a template syntax error.
When a template contains `{% from ... import name, %}`, it should fail with a template syntax error.
When a template contains `{% from ... import name,, %}` or any import list with an empty slot after a comma, it should fail with a template syntax error.
When a template contains a malformed `from ... import ... with context` statement that relies on stray or trailing commas, it should fail with the same syntax validation as the non-context form.

task_12.title: Align indent filter behavior with Jinja 2.10
task_12.description: Jinja 2.10 changes the `indent` filter so blank lines are no longer indented by default, adds an explicit `blank` option to restore the old behavior for empty lines, and renames the first-line indentation argument from `indentfirst` to `first` while keeping the old name as a deprecated alias.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Jinja 2.10 preserves expected template output for the `indent` filter by accounting for the new default of not indenting blank lines, supporting the `first` option for first-line indentation, and handling the deprecated `indentfirst` alias without breaking existing templates.

expectation.grounded: The `indent` filter must expose the 2.10 contract: `width` still controls the indentation width, `first` controls whether the first line is indented, and `blank` controls whether empty lines are indented. By default, calling `indent` must leave the first line and blank lines unindented unless `first=True` or `blank=True` is passed. Calls that still use `indentfirst` must continue to behave like `first` for compatibility, but they must emit a `DeprecationWarning`.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, templates using the `indent` filter should produce output that skips indentation on empty lines unless explicitly requested, continue to support optional first-line indentation through the current API, and warn when older argument naming is used so callers can migrate safely.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress the filter's ability to indent non-empty lines by the requested number of spaces. Do not require callers to opt in for the renamed first-line option when they still pass the legacy alias; compatibility must be preserved with a deprecation signal. Do not indent blank lines unless the caller explicitly enables that behavior through `blank=True`.
constraints.conceptual: Keep existing indentation behavior stable for normal text lines, avoid silently breaking older call sites that still use the previous option name, and make blank-line indentation opt-in rather than the default.

behavior: Applying `indent` with default arguments indents non-empty lines after the first line, but does not indent the first line or blank lines.
Passing `first=True` causes the first line to be indented in addition to the other eligible lines.
Passing `blank=True` causes empty lines to be indented instead of being left empty.
Passing both `first=True` and `blank=True` causes both the first line and blank lines to receive indentation according to `width`.
Passing the legacy `indentfirst` argument remains accepted as an alias for `first`, but it emits a `DeprecationWarning`.
acceptance_criteria: When a multi-line value containing empty lines is rendered through `indent` with default options, blank lines should remain empty while non-empty lines after the first line should still be indented.
When `indent(first=True)` is used, the first rendered line should gain the configured indentation.
When `indent(blank=True)` is used on content that includes empty lines, those empty lines should receive indentation instead of staying blank.
When both `first=True` and `blank=True` are used together, the filter should indent the first line, non-empty subsequent lines, and empty lines consistently by the configured width.
When an existing template uses `indent(indentfirst=...)`, rendering should still apply the corresponding first-line indentation behavior and should also surface a `DeprecationWarning`.

task_13.title: Add reverse ordering support to the dictsort filter
task_13.description: Jinja 2.10 extends the `dictsort` filter with a `reverse` option so templates can request descending dictionary item order while keeping existing key-or-value selection, case-sensitivity behavior, and invalid sort-mode validation.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the `dictsort` filter can return dictionary items in descending order when requested, while preserving its existing ascending default, key-or-value sort selection, case-sensitivity behavior, and invalid sort-mode handling.

expectation.grounded: Expose `dictsort(value, case_sensitive=False, by='key', reverse=False)` as the public filter behavior. The filter should continue to return sorted `(key, value)` pairs, sort by keys by default or by values when `by='value'`, and apply descending order when `reverse=True`. Unsupported `by` values must still raise `FilterArgumentError`.
expectation.conceptual: Templates should be able to ask `dictsort` for either ascending or descending dictionary item order without changing how the filter otherwise works. Users should still be able to choose whether sorting is based on keys or values, and unsupported sort modes should remain explicit errors.

constraints.grounded: Do not change `dictsort` results when `reverse` is omitted or false. Preserve the existing `case_sensitive` contract for comparisons and keep `by` limited to `key` and `value`, with invalid inputs continuing to raise `FilterArgumentError`.
constraints.conceptual: Adding descending sorting must not regress existing ascending behavior, alter established case-sensitivity semantics, or broaden accepted sort-mode inputs beyond the documented choices.

behavior: `dictsort` accepts an additional `reverse` argument.
With `reverse=True`, `dictsort` returns the same `(key, value)` pairs in descending order according to the selected sort target.
With `reverse` omitted or set to `False`, `dictsort` keeps its prior ascending-order behavior.
The `by` argument still determines whether ordering is based on dictionary keys or dictionary values.
Case-insensitive comparison remains the default unless `case_sensitive=True` is provided.
Passing a `by` value other than `key` or `value` continues to raise `FilterArgumentError`.
acceptance_criteria: When `dictsort` is used without `reverse`, it should produce the same ascending ordering behavior as before the upgrade.
When `dictsort(reverse=True)` is used, it should return dictionary items in descending order by key.
When `dictsort(by='value', reverse=True)` is used, it should return dictionary items in descending order by value.
When `case_sensitive` is left at its default, string-based ordering should remain case-insensitive whether sorting by key or value.
When `by` is set to an unsupported option, `dictsort` should raise `FilterArgumentError`.

task_14.title: Add opt-in native Python type rendering
task_14.description: Version 2.10 adds a new opt-in Jinja environment that renders templates to native Python values instead of coercing all output to strings. This lets single-expression templates preserve the original value type and allows some multi-part outputs to be returned as parsed Python literals when their combined rendered form represents a valid native value.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to 2.10 can opt into a template environment that preserves native Python result types during rendering instead of always returning text, so templated values such as numbers, booleans, containers, `None`, and other Python objects can remain usable as native values when the rendered output represents them.

expectation.grounded: Provide `jinja2.nativetypes.NativeEnvironment` as an `Environment` variant whose templates use `NativeTemplate.render()` to return native Python values. For rendered output with no emitted nodes, `render()` should return `None`. For output consisting of a single rendered node, `render()` should return that node's native value directly rather than coercing it to text. For output with multiple emitted nodes, the rendered pieces should be concatenated, then interpreted as a Python literal when possible; if literal parsing succeeds, return the parsed native value, otherwise return the concatenated string. Finalization should still apply, but native rendering must avoid the normal unconditional string conversion step.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should introduce an explicit native-rendering mode for Jinja templates. In that mode, rendering should preserve real Python value types whenever the template output naturally represents a single value or a parseable Python literal, while still falling back to a string for outputs that are genuinely textual.

constraints.grounded: The native-type behavior must be opt-in through `NativeEnvironment` and not redefine the default `Environment` string-rendering contract. Native rendering must continue to honor normal template evaluation and exception handling, including propagation through the environment's standard error handling path. When combined output is not a valid Python literal, the result must remain a string rather than raising a parsing error solely because native conversion was attempted.
constraints.conceptual: Existing text-based template rendering should remain unchanged unless the application explicitly selects the new native mode. Native conversion should be best-effort and safe: preserve normal rendering semantics, keep failures attributable to template evaluation, and treat non-native-looking output as plain text.

behavior: A new `jinja2.nativetypes` module introduces `NativeEnvironment`, `NativeTemplate`, and native-aware output generation for template rendering.
Rendering through `NativeTemplate.render()` can return native Python objects instead of always returning a string.
If a template produces no output nodes, native rendering returns `None`.
If a template's rendered output is a single node, native rendering returns that node's value directly, preserving its Python type.
If a template produces multiple output fragments, they are joined and then interpreted as a Python literal when possible.
If the combined multi-fragment output can be parsed as a Python literal, the parsed native value is returned.
If the combined multi-fragment output cannot be parsed as a Python literal, the rendered result is returned as a string.
Native rendering removes the automatic string coercion normally applied during output generation, while still applying configured finalization logic.
acceptance_criteria: When an application renders a template through `NativeEnvironment` and the template resolves to a single native value, it should receive that value in its original Python type rather than as text.
When a `NativeEnvironment` template emits no output, rendering should return `None`.
When a `NativeEnvironment` template emits multiple fragments whose combined rendered form is a valid Python literal, rendering should return the corresponding native Python value.
When a `NativeEnvironment` template emits multiple fragments whose combined rendered form is not a valid Python literal, rendering should return the combined text.
When applications continue using the standard `Environment`, template rendering should retain the existing string-based behavior.
When template evaluation itself fails during native rendering, the failure should continue to follow the environment's normal exception handling behavior.

task_16.title: Mark `tojson` output as safe markup
task_16.description: Jinja 2.10 changes the `tojson` filter so its HTML-safe JSON output is also marked safe for template rendering. This aligns behavior with the documented contract and prevents autoescaping from re-escaping the serialized JSON syntax while preserving HTML-safe escaping inside the JSON payload.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the `tojson` filter produces JSON that is treated as safe template output, so embedding serialized data in autoescaped templates preserves valid JSON syntax while remaining safe for HTML contexts.

expectation.grounded: The `tojson` filter should return a `Markup` value rather than an ordinary string. Its output should continue to be generated through the existing HTML-safe JSON serialization path, preserving protective escaping for HTML-significant characters in the JSON payload, while preventing a subsequent autoescape pass from escaping the JSON syntax itself.
expectation.conceptual: Serialized JSON produced by `tojson` should behave as already-safe template content. Users should be able to embed JSON in autoescaped templates without the serializer output being transformed into HTML-escaped text, and without losing the safety protections needed for HTML embedding.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the JSON serialization contract beyond safety marking. `tojson` must still honor the configured dumper and serialization options, and it must retain HTML-safe escaping of characters that could affect embedding in HTML.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should only change how `tojson` is treated by template escaping, not what data gets serialized or how custom JSON serialization behavior is selected. Safety protections for HTML embedding must remain in place.

behavior: `tojson` now yields safe markup instead of plain text.
In autoescaped template rendering, `tojson` output is no longer escaped a second time as normal text.
HTML-significant characters that the JSON-safe serializer already protects remain escaped within the rendered JSON payload.
Any configured custom JSON dumper behavior still applies before the result is exposed as safe markup.
acceptance_criteria: When a template renders a value with `tojson` in an autoescaped environment, it should emit JSON syntax directly rather than HTML entity-escaped JSON punctuation or quotes.
When serialized content contains characters that are unsafe to embed directly in HTML, the rendered JSON should still encode them in an HTML-safe form.
When application code relies on the filter result's safety status, `tojson` output should be recognized as safe markup rather than ordinary text.
When `tojson` is used with custom JSON serialization configuration, that configuration should still control the serialized content while the final output remains marked safe.

task_17.title: Prevent traceback debug locals from mutating Jinja template context
task_17.description: The upgrade fixes a bug in Jinja 2.10 where collecting debug locals for traceback translation could accidentally mutate the active template context. Debug and exception inspection should now operate on a snapshot of context data so template state is preserved.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that retrieving traceback debug locals in Jinja does not modify the active template context while still exposing the current template variables for debugging.

expectation.grounded: When Jinja gathers locals for traceback handling through its debug-local extraction path, including `get_jinja_locals`, it should read from the current `context` without returning or mutating the live mapping produced from `context.get_all()`. The debug locals should behave as an isolated snapshot of the template variables visible at the time of the exception.
expectation.conceptual: Debugging a template failure should never change the template's own variable state. The locals shown for a traceback should reflect the template context at the moment of failure, but they must be detached from the live context so inspection remains side-effect free.

constraints.grounded: Preserve the existing ability to expose template variables from the active context during traceback translation. If no template context is present, local extraction should still produce an empty set of template locals rather than failing. The fix must not require callers to change how they trigger or consume traceback translation.
constraints.conceptual: Keep traceback debugging behavior compatible for callers while removing unintended side effects. Debug information should still be available, and absence of template context should continue to be handled safely.

behavior: Traceback debug-local collection uses a copy of the template context data instead of the live context mapping.
Inspecting or augmenting the locals used for Jinja traceback translation no longer writes back into the active template context.
When a template context exists, the reported debug locals still include the variables currently visible in that context.
When no template context is available, debug-local extraction continues to return an empty mapping of template locals.
acceptance_criteria: When a template exception is translated into a Jinja traceback and template context is present, the reported locals should contain the current template variables without altering the template context itself.
When internal traceback processing adds or adjusts entries in the debug locals mapping, those changes should not appear in the live template context.
When traceback debug locals are requested without an active template context, the operation should complete safely and provide no template-local entries.

task_15.title: Support filtered block set assignments
task_15.description: Jinja 2.10 extends the block-form `set` tag so captured block content can be passed through standard filter syntax before assignment. The rendered value still follows the active autoescape behavior, and `set` target parsing is broadened to accept namespace-qualified targets in supported assignment forms.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that block-form `set` assignments can apply standard Jinja filters to captured content before storing the result, while preserving normal escaping behavior and supporting namespace-qualified `set` targets.

expectation.grounded: The `set` tag should accept an optional filter clause in block form and carry that parsed filter on `AssignBlock`. When rendering a block assignment, the captured block output should be concatenated, passed through the declared filter chain if one is present, and then wrapped according to the current autoescape evaluation context before assignment to the target. `parse_set` should also allow namespace-qualified assignment targets for `set`, including block assignments.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.10 should be able to write a block `set` that transforms its captured content with normal Jinja filters before the value is stored. The resulting assigned value should behave like normal rendered template content with respect to escaping, and namespace-style `set` targets should be accepted where `set` assignments are supported.

constraints.grounded: Existing unfiltered block `set` behavior must remain unchanged. Adding filters to block `set` must not bypass or duplicate existing autoescape handling. Expression-style `set` assignments should retain their prior behavior except for expanded acceptance of namespace-qualified targets during `set` parsing.
constraints.conceptual: Templates that do not use this new syntax should continue to behave the same. The new capability should only add filtered block assignment behavior and broader supported target syntax without introducing escaping regressions.

behavior: Block-form `set` accepts an optional filter chain after the assignment target and before the block body.
When a filter chain is present on a block `set`, the assigned value is the filtered form of the captured block content rather than the raw concatenated block output.
The final assigned value from a filtered block `set` still respects the active autoescape context.
`set` target parsing accepts namespace-qualified targets in addition to plain names, including for block assignment form.
acceptance_criteria: When a template uses block `set` with a filter clause, rendering should assign the transformed block content to the target instead of the unfiltered captured text.
When multiple standard Jinja filters are chained on a block `set`, rendering should apply them in normal filter order before assignment.
When autoescaping is enabled, using filters on a block `set` should preserve normal escaping behavior for dynamic content in the assigned value.
When a `set` statement targets a namespace-qualified name, both expression and block forms should be accepted and assign to that namespace target.

task_18.title: Support large Jinja elif chains without compilation failure
task_18.description: Jinja 2.10 fixes template compilation for long `{% if %}` / `{% elif %}` chains by treating `elif` as a first-class branch during parsing and code generation instead of nesting it as an `else` followed by another `if`. This removes indentation-depth compilation failures while preserving normal branch selection and fallback behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates containing large numbers of `{% elif %}` branches compile and render successfully without failing due to generated indentation depth, while preserving the normal ordered behavior of `if` / `elif` / `else` branch evaluation.

expectation.grounded: Templates using Jinja `if` blocks with one or more `{% elif %}` clauses should compile such that each `elif` is represented as a distinct branch of `jinja2.nodes.If` via `elif_`, and code generation should emit native `elif` branches rather than nesting additional `If` nodes inside `else_`. Rendering must continue to evaluate the initial `if`, then each `elif_` in order, then `else_` only if no condition matches. Branch symbol tracking must include assignments and references from `body`, `elif_`, and `else_` as parallel alternatives.
expectation.conceptual: A template author should be able to write long `if` / `elif` chains without hitting an internal compiler limit. The engine should treat each `elif` as part of the same decision chain, choose the first matching branch in order, and fall back to `else` only when nothing matches.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the observable truth-testing order or fallback semantics of Jinja conditional blocks. `else_` must remain the final fallback branch, and `elif_` branches must participate in the same branch-analysis rules as the main `if` body and `else_`. Templates without `elif` must continue to behave the same as before.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should remove the failure mode for deep conditional chains without changing which content renders for existing templates or altering how ordinary `if` / `else` blocks behave.

behavior: A template with many consecutive `{% elif %}` clauses should compile successfully instead of failing with an indentation-depth error during template compilation.
Each `{% elif %}` branch should be treated as an ordered sibling branch of the original conditional, not as a nested conditional inside the `else` path.
During rendering, Jinja should evaluate the initial `if` condition first, then each `elif` condition in source order, and render the first matching branch.
If none of the `if` or `elif` conditions match, Jinja should render the `else` branch when one is present.
Branch-aware symbol tracking should account for names assigned or referenced in `elif` branches the same way it does for the main `if` body and the `else` branch.
acceptance_criteria: When a template contains a long `if` / `elif` chain, compiling or rendering it should not fail because the generated Python code exceeds indentation depth limits.
When an early `if` condition is false and a later `elif` condition is true, rendering should produce the content of that matching `elif` branch.
When none of the `if` or `elif` conditions are true and an `else` branch exists, rendering should produce the `else` content.

When a conditional block includes `elif` branches, the template engine should preserve the same external behavior as a normal ordered `if` / `elif` / `else` chain regardless of how many `elif` clauses are present.

When code inspects or relies on Jinja's conditional branch structure, `elif` alternatives should be represented distinctly from the final `else` fallback and participate in branch analysis consistently.
